quote: Kann die geschlossene Linie (Cykel) Wendepunkte haben?
english: Can the closed curve (cycle) have inflection points?
topic: A list of research and dissertation topics: the discriminant and invariants of the quartic, Poincaré cycles of differential equations, rotation of a body filled with fluid, three number-theoretic doctoral topics (class fields, Fermat's theorem, Weber's theorem), and independence of the laws 1-17 for complex number systems.

triage.modern_statement: Take a planar polynomial (Poincaré-type) differential system dx/dt = P(x,y), dy/dt = Q(x,y). Can one of its closed orbits (a 'cycle' or limit cycle in Poincaré's sense) be non-convex, meaning its curvature changes sign so that it has inflection points? A natural refinement asks whether the answer depends on the degree of P and Q.
triage.answered_by: My search confirmed only one point. For quadratic systems (degree 2), it is now standard that every periodic orbit is convex, so these orbits have no inflection points. A 2022 arXiv paper on limit cycles states this as known. From background knowledge, not checked against sources, I attribute the result to the Chinese school of the late 1950s (Tung Chin-Chu, 1959) and to Coppel's 1966 survey of quadratic systems. For systems of degree 3 or higher, my background knowledge is that non-convex cycles with inflection points do occur. I could not confirm either the attribution or the higher-degree claim because I ran out of searches.

evidence.claim: A 2022 paper on the number of limit cycles of planar systems states that 'it is known that periodic orbits of QS [quadratic systems] are convex'.
Background on Poincaré's limit cycles for planar polynomial vector fields and how they relate to Hilbert's 16th problem.

triage.why: The note sits in a list of dissertation topics next to 'Poincaré cycles of differential equations', so 'Cykel' almost certainly means Poincaré's closed trajectories, and the question is whether they can have inflection points. I found one source showing that the quadratic case was settled: those cycles are always convex. I did not confirm who proved it or when, and I found no source for higher degrees. I also could not establish which class of equations Hilbert had in mind, so the overall answer may depend on the degree. This is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. It is a side question related to the 16th problem (limit cycles). Convexity of cycles comes up in that literature as a known fact, not as a research topic in its own right, so I can't say whether it is active today.
